answers.question: How much capital funding could Berkeley redirect to streets?
answers.headline: Little can be shown to be available. Fund 501 could free at most $2,946,000 over two years, only by delaying every other project it pays for; that is a budget ceiling, not cash. Whether Measure FF could add more is an open legal question.
key_uncertainties: The $2,946,000 is money budgeted for other projects, not money known to be unspent. Public records do not show how much is already under contract or spent.
Freeing it means delaying roof, building, pool, sidewalk and other repairs. BeTH has not assessed what those delays would cost.
Measure FF says "approximately" 45% for streets. Whether that allows more paving without a vote has not been settled by the City Attorney or Council.

resolution.scope: CIP Fund 501 and Measure FF only. Other capital funds (sewer, storm water, zero waste, parks tax, state and county transportation funds, internal service funds) are not yet assessed here.

answers.short_answer: From CIP Fund 501: a gross conditional ceiling of $2,946,000 of FY2027-FY2028 appropriations, or $2,916,000 excluding a contractual Joint Powers Agreement contribution. It is reached only by deferring or cancelling every other project the fund pays for, and neither figure is verified available cash. 88% of the fund's FY2027 money ($10,412,200) already goes to paving. A one-time amount from unspent carried-over appropriations may exist but cannot be measured from public records; its ceiling at June 30, 2025 was $11,568,647. From Measure FF: the adopted program already puts 45.6% into street rehabilitation, against a voter-set allocation of "approximately" 45% that Council cannot alter without a vote. Whether more could go to paving without a vote is an unresolved legal question, and BeTH states no amount.

The minimum limits moving paving money out of streets, not into them.

answers.question: Could Measure FF money pay for more street paving?
answers.headline: Unclear. Voters fixed Measure FF's split at about 45% for streets, and the adopted plan already puts 45.6% into street repaving. Whether more could go to paving without a vote is an open legal question.
key_uncertainties: The ordinance says "approximately" 45% for streets. It does not say how much room that allows.
It does not say whether the split must be met every year or over the 14-year life of the tax.
No City Attorney opinion on these questions is in the public records BeTH holds.
answers.short_answer: Not established. Voters set the split at approximately 45% streets, 15% sidewalks and paths, 30% safety and 10% environmental and other uses, and Council cannot alter it without a vote. The adopted program already puts 45.6% of Measure FF ($42,119,935 of $92,282,816) into street rehabilitation. Whether Council could put more into paving without a vote turns on unresolved legal questions: how much room "approximately" allows, whether the shares apply each year or over the life of the tax, and how revenue not yet programmed may be used. BeTH states no amount.

cite.quote: Tax proceeds shall be allocated approximately as follows: 1) 60% for streets and sidewalks, of which roughly three quarters (45%) will be for streets and one quarter (15%) will be for sidewalks and pedestrian paths, until the backlog of damaged sidewalks and pedestrian paths is eliminated. 2) 30% for safety improvements. 3) The remaining 10% shall include environmental enhancements

interpretation.text: The adopted program is already at the ordinance's approximate street share, so more Measure FF paving would have to come from the latitude "approximately" allows or from revenue not yet programmed. How large that latitude is cannot be settled from the ordinance text.
interpretation.counterargument: A strict reading, with the shares binding each year's appropriations, leaves little or no room. A looser reading, with the shares measured over the 14-year life of the tax, could allow more paving in early years balanced later. No City Attorney opinion in BeTH's sources settles which applies.

open_interpretations: How much room the word "approximately" in "approximately 45%" allows, and who decides.
Whether the percentages must be met every year, over the five-year plan, or over the 14-year life of the tax.
Whether the ordinance's "streets" share means the same thing as the budget's "street rehabilitation" line, or also covers street work paid for from the safety or environmental shares.
How the City may use FY2027 revenue that came in above the adopted plan, and FY2026 collections not yet budgeted. Neither has been assigned in the documents BeTH holds.

The ordinance says the percentage rules end when the citywide average PCI reaches 70, but the sentence that says so points to the wrong subsection (7.11.020(D) refers to 7.11.030(C)). This is probably a drafting error, and its effect is not settled.
No City Attorney opinion or Council interpretation of these provisions is in BeTH's sources.

answers.question: How bad are Berkeley's streets, beyond the average PCI?
answers.headline: Worse than the average suggests. The 2024 average was PCI 56 out of 100, but 88.5 miles of streets, 42% of the network, were below PCI 50.
key_uncertainties: The data are from 2024 inspections, before the last two years of paving.
The City reports a related but different figure: 41.93% of pavement area in "poor" or "failed" condition. It measures area rather than length, and includes streets at exactly PCI 50.
The City publishes no forecast of how many streets will still be below PCI 50 in future years.

resolution.scope: Mileage is computed from section lengths in feet and reported to 0.1 mile. One uninspected 155-foot section (Tevlin St, PCI 0, no inspection date) is excluded, as in the report's totals table.

answers.short_answer: The average hides most of it. In the 2024 inspection the network averaged PCI 56, but 88.5 centerline miles (42% of the network) were below PCI 50 and 33.9 miles were below 25. The City projects an average of about 62 by 2038 with Measure FF, but publishes no projection of how many streets will still be below 50. The adopted plans treat 22.6 miles of currently-below-50 streets over five years.

cite.quote: The updated Pavement Management Program showed that the City's overall average PCI is 56.

interpretation.text: Reaching a network average of 60 or 62 is not the same as eliminating failed streets; the measure that matches Measure FF's goal is the mileage below PCI 50.
interpretation.counterargument: Treating the worst streets first costs more per point of average PCI (the City shows about one point lower in 2038), so a lower failed-street count can mean a lower average; both measures are needed.

missing_evidence.needed: Projected miles below PCI 50 under each funding scenario.
missing_evidence.would_be_in: StreetSaver output; the Measure FF annual report must include "the PCI of all streets" (BMC 7.11.050(B)(1))

open_interpretations: The City's 41.93% and BeTH's 88.5 miles measure different things. The City's figure is pavement area rated "poor" or "failed" (PCI 50 and below); BeTH's figure is street length below PCI 50.
BeTH measured length from each section's length in feet. Adding up the report's rounded mileage figures instead gives slightly more. Figures are shown to a tenth of a mile.
One short section of Tevlin Street was not inspected and has no score. BeTH leaves it out, as the report's totals do; the report's condition table counts it as failed.
The data are from 2024 inspections, before the City's FY2025-FY2026 paving.

Street scores in the City's plans are the scores when the plans were written; streets will be in worse condition by the time they are repaved. The 22.6 miles are streets now below 50 that the plans list for work.

answers.question: What does the $139.3 million streets figure include?
answers.headline: It is a five-year figure, not a two-year one. The $139,356,147 covers FY2027 through FY2031; the two-year amount is $58,211,462.
key_uncertainties: The last three years, FY2029-FY2031, are plans, not approved spending, and may change.
Some one-time street-related money added with the Mayor's budget recommendations is outside this table.
answers.short_answer: It is the five-year (FY2027-FY2031) Streets capital budget, not a two-year one: the paving plan ($96,336,212), Measure FF street rehabilitation ($42,119,935), bridge maintenance and Harold Way placemaking add to exactly $139,356,147. The two-year FY2027-FY2028 Streets amount is $58,211,462.

interpretation.text: Comparisons that treat $139,356,147 as a biennial figure overstate two-year street spending by more than double. (The figure in the question is slightly low: the exact amount rounds to $139.4 million.)
interpretation.counterargument: FY2029-FY2031 are planned amounts and may change; the two-year figure is the only one with appropriations behind it.

open_interpretations: BeTH has not found the source of the figure in the question. The exact five-year amount rounds to $139.4 million, and the City's street plan describes it as "over $139 million".
The last three years, FY2029-FY2031, are plans, not approved spending.
Some one-time money added with the Mayor's budget recommendations, including funding for Oxford for All, is outside the Streets table. Whether it belongs in a "streets figure" is a judgment call.
Changes Council made at the June 23, 2026 meeting, and the FY2027 Annual Appropriation Ordinance, are not in BeTH's sources.
